graph.summary: Thiamine → Thiamine pyrophosphate → Transketolase → Carbohydrate metabolism → Avitaminosis

evidence.snippet: Once thiamine enters the cells it is phosphorylated by thiamine pyrophosphokinase (TPPK), and converted into the coenzyme thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), the active form of thiamine.
evidence.explanation: Thiamine is phosphorylated intracellularly and converted into its active metabolite, thiamine pyrophosphate.

evidence.snippet: TPP is a relevant cofactor for transketolase (TK), α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (αKDH), and pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH), all these enzymes are fundamental for glucose metabolism.
evidence.explanation: Thiamine pyrophosphate serves as the coenzyme/cofactor required for transketolase activity.

evidence.snippet: TPP is a relevant cofactor for transketolase (TK), α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (αKDH), and pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH), all these enzymes are fundamental for glucose metabolism.
evidence.explanation: Transketolase is one of the thiamine-dependent enzymes fundamental for glucose/carbohydrate metabolism.

evidence.snippet: Thiamine is an essential cofactor in carbohydrate metabolism, and deficiency can therefore cause various organ dysfunctions.
evidence.explanation: Functional thiamine-dependent carbohydrate metabolism is inversely related to the deficiency disease: it is the loss/impairment of this metabolism when thiamine is deficient (avitaminosis) that produces the organ dysfunctions constituting the disease.
